nigeria.anchor: an ice sachet melting in your hand

us.anchor: an ice cube left out on the counter

cards.title: Particles never stop
cards.body: Even in solid ice, particles are vibrating. They slow down when cooled — but they never fully stop.

cards.title: Heat = particle energy
cards.body: Adding heat makes particles move faster and push further apart. Remove heat — they slow down and pull closer.

cards.title: How to Play
cards.body: Drag the temperature slider up to heat, down to cool. When particles change behaviour, tap the label that matches what you see.

missions.title: The Frozen Sample
missions.learningGoal: Particles in a solid vibrate in fixed positions; adding energy lets them slide past each other — that is melting.

transitions.correctLabel: Particles breaking free of each other
options: Particles breaking free of each other
Particles vibrating faster in place
Particles escaping from the surface
Particles locking into fixed positions
Particles disappearing into the air
Particles slowing down and pulling together
transitions.confirmationNarration: Exactly. They were already vibrating — you gave them enough energy to slide past each other. That is melting. The substance is still water. Nothing was destroyed.

wrongFeedback.Particles vibrating faster in place: They are moving faster — you noticed that. But watch the gaps between them. Are they still locked to the same spot, or are they starting to pass through each other?
wrongFeedback.Particles escaping from the surface: Surface escape is a different event — that would be evaporation. Right now watch the entire group of particles, not just the edges.
wrongFeedback.Particles locking into fixed positions: You would see that if you were cooling, not heating. Check the slider direction — you have been adding heat.
wrongFeedback.Particles disappearing into the air: Look at the canvas and count — did any particles actually disappear? The number stays the same throughout every change of state.
wrongFeedback.Particles slowing down and pulling toget: Slowing down and pulling together happens when you remove heat. You are adding heat here. Watch which direction the particles are moving relative to each other.

missions.title: Steam Pressure
missions.learningGoal: Removing energy from a gas causes particles to slow and pull together — that is condensation, the reverse of evaporation.

transitions.correctLabel: Particles slowing down and pulling together
options: Particles slowing down and pulling together
Particles breaking free of each other
Particles disappearing
Particles locking into fixed positions
Particles escaping from the surface
Particles vibrating faster in place
transitions.confirmationNarration: Right. You removed energy — the particles slowed down enough for attraction to pull them together. Gas became liquid. This is condensation. The same particles, just closer and slower.

wrongFeedback.Particles breaking free of each other: Breaking free happens when you add energy, not remove it. You are cooling the sample — watch the slider direction.
wrongFeedback.Particles disappearing: Count the dots. None of them vanished — they are just rearranging. Matter is conserved through every change of state.
wrongFeedback.Particles locking into fixed positions: Locking into position would be freezing — a further cooling step. At this threshold, the particles are gaining enough attraction to move together, but they are not fixed yet.
wrongFeedback.Particles escaping from the surface: Surface escape is evaporation, which happens when heating. Here you are cooling and the particles are coming together, not leaving.
wrongFeedback.Particles vibrating faster in place: Faster vibration happens when you add heat. You are removing heat here — watch what the particles are doing to each other.

missions.title: Full Cycle
missions.learningGoal: There are two distinct transition thresholds — one where solid becomes liquid, one where liquid becomes gas — and mass is conserved at both.

transitions.correctLabel: Particles breaking free of each other
options: Particles breaking free of each other
Particles vibrating faster in place
Particles escaping from the surface
Particles slowing down and pulling together
transitions.confirmationNarration: Melting — the particles gained enough energy to slide past each other. Keep heating to find the next change.

wrongFeedback.Particles vibrating faster in place: They are vibrating faster, yes — but are they still stuck to the same positions, or are they now passing through each other?
wrongFeedback.Particles escaping from the surface: Surface escape would be evaporation. Look at all the particles, not just those on the outer edge.
wrongFeedback.Particles slowing down and pulling toget: That is the opposite direction. You are heating, not cooling.

transitions.correctLabel: Particles throughout the liquid gaining enough energy to form gas
options: Particles throughout the liquid gaining enough energy to form gas
Only the fastest surface particles leaving
Particles breaking free of each other
Particles disappearing
transitions.confirmationNarration: Boiling. The entire liquid — not just the surface — now has enough energy to become gas. Every particle eventually escapes. This is different from evaporation, which happens only at the surface.

wrongFeedback.Only the fastest surface particles leavi: That would be evaporation — a surface-only event that can happen at any temperature. Boiling is different. Watch — it is happening throughout the whole liquid, not just the top.
wrongFeedback.Particles breaking free of each other: Breaking free of each other was melting — the first transition. Something bigger is happening now: the entire liquid is turning to gas, not just rearranging into a liquid.
wrongFeedback.Particles disappearing: The particles are still there — they have just spread so far apart they are in the gas state. Count them before and after.

missions.title: The Surface Mystery
missions.learningGoal: Evaporation happens only at the surface and only for the fastest-moving particles — it can occur at any temperature, not just at boiling point.

transitions.correctLabel: Only the fastest surface particles escaping
options: Only the fastest surface particles escaping
All particles gaining enough energy to become gas
Particles breaking free of each other throughout
Particles disappearing from the edges
transitions.confirmationNarration: That is evaporation. Only the fastest-moving particles near the surface have enough energy to escape. The rest of the liquid stays liquid. This is why wet clothes dry in the sun without boiling.

wrongFeedback.All particles gaining enough energy to b: That would be boiling — the whole liquid converting to gas at once. Here the temperature is well below boiling point. Look at where the escaping particles are coming from.
wrongFeedback.Particles breaking free of each other th: Breaking free throughout was melting. The sample is already liquid. Only a small number of particles are leaving — and only from one place. Where exactly?
wrongFeedback.Particles disappearing from the edges: They are not disappearing — they are escaping into the gas phase. And it is not the edges generally, but specifically the surface. What is special about the particles that leave?

missions.title: Mothballs
missions.learningGoal: Some substances transition directly from solid to gas — the expected melting event never occurs, and no liquid phase appears.

transitions.correctLabel: Particles going directly from solid to gas
options: Particles going directly from solid to gas
Particles breaking free of each other
Particles escaping only from the surface
Particles gaining energy before melting first
Particles disappearing
Particles slowly forming a liquid
transitions.confirmationNarration: Sublimation. No liquid phase appeared at all. Some substances — like naphthalene in mothballs — have inter-particle forces that allow a direct solid-to-gas transition. The particles themselves are unchanged. Only their arrangement changed.

wrongFeedback.Particles breaking free of each other: Breaking free of each other is what happens in melting — but watch the canvas. Did a liquid phase appear? The particles went from fixed-position jitter straight to free movement with large gaps. That skipped the liquid entirely.
wrongFeedback.Particles escaping only from the surface: Surface escape at lower temperatures would be evaporation — and that requires a liquid surface. Here there was no liquid at any point. Look at the state before and after.
wrongFeedback.Particles gaining energy before melting: That is what you would expect — but look at what actually happened. The melting transition never fired. The threshold you passed was different.
wrongFeedback.Particles disappearing: Count the particles before and after. The number is the same — they have not disappeared, they are just very far apart and moving very fast.
wrongFeedback.Particles slowly forming a liquid: A liquid was never formed. Watch the particle arrangement — it went from the tight grid directly to the sparse fast-moving pattern of a gas.

missions.title: Explain the Puddle
missions.learningGoal: Condensation can occur when ambient gas particles lose energy on contact with a cold surface — no prior liquid is needed.

transitions.correctLabel: Particles losing energy near the cold surface and becoming liquid
options: Particles losing energy near the cold surface and becoming liquid
Particles disappearing when they touch the surface
Particles breaking free as they hit the cold surface
Particles freezing into solid on the surface
New water particles appearing from nowhere
Particles slowing throughout the whole container
transitions.confirmationNarration: Condensation from ambient vapour. The gas particles in the air lost energy when they contacted the cold surface — enough for attraction to pull them together into liquid droplets. That is the water on the outside of a cold bottle. The water was already in the air.

wrongFeedback.Particles disappearing when they touch t: They did not disappear. Look — the particle count stays the same. They are joining together on the surface as liquid, not vanishing.
wrongFeedback.Particles breaking free as they hit the: Breaking free requires energy gain. The cold surface removes energy. Watch what happens to particle speed near the surface.
wrongFeedback.Particles freezing into solid on the sur: Freezing would require much lower temperatures. At this threshold the particles are becoming liquid, not solid. The arrangement changes, but not into a rigid grid.
wrongFeedback.New water particles appearing from nowhe: Matter cannot be created. The water droplets forming on the surface came from gas particles already present in the air — they did not appear from nothing.
wrongFeedback.Particles slowing throughout the whole c: Only the particles near the cold surface slow enough to condense. The rest of the gas away from the surface continues moving freely. This is a surface effect, like evaporation.
